title: The Arctic Town Anyone Can Move To. Bring a Rifle.
question: Why do people live in Longyearbyen?
message: This video tells curious adults that the northernmost town of its size exists because of coal and a treaty, and stays alive after coal by becoming a town of scientists, guides and seeds, open to anyone who can support themselves.
angle: People live in Longyearbyen because an American tourist turned a coal seam into a mining town and a nineteen twenty treaty opened it to people from everywhere, and now research, tourism and the seed vault keep it going after the last mine closed, despite four months of polar night, polar bears beyond the town edge, scarce housing and ground so frozen the cemetery stopped taking burials.

scenes.narration: The town is Longyearbyen, on Svalbard, a group of Arctic islands belonging to Norway, about halfway between the mainland and the North Pole. It is the northernmost settlement in the world with more than a thousand people. There are no trees. There are plenty of polar bears just outside town. And because of a treaty signed more than a century ago, almost anyone can move here without a visa. Coal built it, and coal is gone. So by the end of this trip I wanted to know a couple of things. Why did anyone come to begin with, and why do they keep coming now? I packed every warm thing I own, plus a few things I borrowed. I still underpacked.

scenes.chapter: Flying to the Top of the Map
scenes.role: chương 1: bay tới, cảnh quan không cây, nhà trên cột
scenes.narration: I flew north from the Norwegian mainland and kept drawing my route in my notebook until the map ran out of land. Out of the window: white mountains with flat tops, sea ice, and then a valley with a little town in it. Colourful wooden houses, many of them standing on posts above the ground. The ground here is permafrost, frozen all year round, and you do not want your warm house melting it. The airport is a short ride from town. On the way in I saw old wooden towers marching up the hillside, the remains of cableways that once carried coal. The whole valley looked like a museum that someone had forgotten to close, with people still living in it.

scenes.chapter: A Town Named After a Tourist
scenes.role: chương 2: Wob đoán (nghiên cứu/khoa học) → lý do thật: than, John Munro Longyear du lịch 1901, mỏ 1906
scenes.narration: So who decided to build a town up here? My guess was scientists. Polar research, important instruments, people in thick jackets measuring things. Good guess. Wrong century. The real answer is a tourist. In nineteen oh one, an American businessman called John Munro Longyear came to Svalbard on a cruise with his family. He met people prospecting for coal, took samples home, and liked what he found. In nineteen oh six his Arctic Coal Company started mining here. The town was called Longyear City until nineteen twenty-six. Picture going on a cruise, buying a souvenir, and the souvenir turning out to be a mine with your name on it.

scenes.role: Store Norske mua 1916, nhà nước Na Uy; một thế kỷ than; Mine 7 đóng 6/2025
scenes.narration: The American company ran into money trouble, and in nineteen sixteen the Norwegian company Store Norske bought the mines. The Norwegian state became an owner in the nineteen thirties and now owns the company outright. For more than a hundred years, coal was the reason this town had lights, heat and jobs. Then the world changed. At the end of June twenty twenty-five, Mine Seven, the last Norwegian coal mine on Svalbard, closed. I held my lump of coal and stood outside the old mine entrance. It felt like visiting a house where the family has just moved out, and nobody has told the cat.

scenes.chapter: The Treaty That Opens the Door
scenes.role: chương 3: Hiệp ước 1920; quyền bình đẳng; không visa nhưng phải tự nuôi mình; nhà ở
scenes.narration: Here is the part that surprised me most. In February nineteen twenty, a treaty signed in Paris recognised Norway's sovereignty over Svalbard, but with conditions. Norway has to treat citizens and companies from the countries that signed it equally. Today the treaty has forty-eight parties. And in practice, according to the Governor of Svalbard, you do not need a visa or a Norwegian residence permit to come here. The Norwegian Immigration Act does not apply. Picture a shared garden with one rule on the gate. Anyone may come in, as long as they bring their own lunch. Because here is the catch. You must be able to support yourself. Most housing is provided by employers, nearly all the land belongs to the state, and the Governor can turn away people who do not meet the requirements. So the door is open. It is just very cold on the doorstep.

scenes.narration: On my second day I decided to go for a nice walk out of town, toward the mountains. I got as far as a sign. A red triangle, with a polar bear on it. I stopped. I looked at the bear on the sign. The bear on the sign looked back. I read the rules that evening, from somewhere warm. According to the Governor of Svalbard, anyone travelling outside the settlements must carry suitable means of scaring off polar bears, and the Governor also recommends carrying a firearm. Inside town, you can walk to the shop in peace. Beyond the sign, you are in the bears' neighbourhood. I went back the next morning on an organised trip with a guide who knew exactly what to do. I knew exactly how to stand behind the guide. Teamwork.

scenes.role: chương 5 (không gag): nghĩa trang 1918, cúm Tây Ban Nha, ngừng chôn ~1950, sửa chuyện 'chết là phạm luật'; thị trấn bị phá 1943
scenes.narration: There is a small cemetery on the hillside above town, with white crosses. I want to tell this part plainly. Seven miners who died in the Spanish flu pandemic of nineteen eighteen are buried there. Because of the permafrost, bodies in this ground do not decompose the way they would elsewhere, and the frozen soil slowly pushes coffins upward. Since around nineteen fifty, the cemetery has not taken new burials, and people who die here are taken to the mainland to be buried. You may have heard that dying is illegal in Longyearbyen. It is not. It is simply that the ground here keeps everything. In the late nineteen nineties, researchers even studied the remains of those miners, hoping to learn about the flu virus. The town has known hard days in other ways too. On the eighth of September, nineteen forty-three, the German navy almost completely destroyed it. It was rebuilt after the war.

scenes.role: chương 6: từ một hạt giống → kho hạt giống (2008, >1 triệu mẫu) → nghiên cứu, du lịch; thị trấn đổi nghề
scenes.narration: So if coal is gone, what keeps the lights on? I asked myself this while my own lights, the ones in my head, were running low on hot chocolate. Start with a single seed. Small enough to lose in your pocket. Zoom out: a box of seeds, sealed and labelled. Zoom out again. I stood in the snow outside a tunnel cut deep into the mountain above the airport. This is where the Svalbard Global Seed Vault has kept backup copies of the world's crop seeds since it opened in twenty oh eight. It now holds more than a million seed samples, according to the vault's own figures quoted by travel guides. Think of it as the backup drive for the world's farms, stored somewhere naturally cold. Zoom out once more: a town of researchers, students, guides and hotel staff. The University Centre in Svalbard brings students to study the Arctic. Tourism brings visitors for the midnight sun, the northern lights and the glaciers. The town did not stop when the coal stopped. It changed jobs.

scenes.role: đời sống: để giày ở cửa, mọi thứ 'cực bắc'; Wob đổi ý lần 1
scenes.narration: Daily life here has its own little habits. People often take their shoes off at the door, even in shops and hotels, and pad around in socks or slippers. There is a hospital, a school and a sports centre, all of which can claim to be the northernmost of their kind. There are no roads connecting Svalbard's settlements, so people travel between them by boat, small plane or snowmobile. I spent an evening in a café in my socks, drinking hot chocolate. I watched people come in from the cold with frost on their eyebrows and stamp their boots like happy horses. Everyone seemed to have arrived from somewhere else, for a job, a research project, or a season that turned into years. I changed my mind. I could see myself in my socks here.

scenes.narration: Then I came back in winter, and the town was in darkness. In Longyearbyen the polar night lasts from about the twenty-sixth of October until about the fifteenth of February. For weeks, the sun simply does not come up. The streetlights do the work, and the northern lights, when they appear, do the showing off. I went outside at noon and it looked like midnight. I went outside at midnight and it looked like noon's darker cousin. Then I came back again in summer, and the opposite happened. The midnight sun lasts from about the twentieth of April until about the twenty-third of August. I tried to sleep and the sun stood outside my window like a neighbour who wants to chat. I put foil on the glass. The sun found the gaps. Winter tested me. Summer charmed me. I changed my mind again, and then back, which is apparently normal here.

scenes.chapter: Would I Move to the Top of the Map?
scenes.role: về bàn: ghép các mảnh 'vì sao', phán quyết WOULD MOVE có điều kiện, callback cục than, câu hỏi kéo bình luận
scenes.narration: So here is how the coal adds up. A tourist found coal and started a mine. A treaty opened the islands to people from many countries. When the coal ran out, the town traded mines for science, seeds and visitors, and kept going. The price is real: months of darkness, bears beyond the sign, scarce housing and a frozen ground that keeps everything. Would I move there? Yes. My verdict is WOULD MOVE, if I can find a job and somewhere to live, which, up here, is the whole question. It suits curious people who like cold air, long projects and taking their shoes off. It does not suit anyone who needs trees, or a walk without a rifle. I put the coal next to the seed on my desk. One kept the town alive for a century. The other is keeping it alive now. What would you need to move to the top of the map?

verdict.label: WOULD MOVE
verdict.reason: A town anyone may move to, full of people who chose it, worth the polar night and the bears, as long as you can find work and a place to live.

claims.quote: The mine it came from closed in twenty twenty-five, after more than a century of digging.
claims.statement: Mine 7, the last Norwegian coal mine on Svalbard, closed in 2025, ending more than 100 years of Norwegian coal mining there.

claims.quote: The town is Longyearbyen, on Svalbard, a group of Arctic islands belonging to Norway, about halfway between the mainland and the North Pole. It is the northernmost settlement in the world with more than a thousand people.
claims.statement: Longyearbyen, on Norway's Svalbard archipelago roughly halfway between mainland Norway and the North Pole, is the world's northernmost settlement with a population greater than 1,000.

claims.quote: There are no trees. There are plenty of polar bears just outside town.
claims.statement: There are no trees in Longyearbyen, and polar bears roam outside the settlements of Svalbard.

claims.quote: And because of a treaty signed more than a century ago, almost anyone can move here without a visa.
claims.statement: Under the 1920 Svalbard Treaty framework, no visa or Norwegian residence permit is needed to live in Svalbard, though residents must be able to support themselves.

claims.quote: The ground here is permafrost, frozen all year round, and you do not want your warm house melting it.
claims.statement: Longyearbyen is built on permafrost, ground that stays frozen year-round, and many buildings stand on posts.

claims.quote: On the way in I saw old wooden towers marching up the hillside, the remains of cableways that once carried coal.
claims.statement: Remains of old cableways that carried coal from mines stand on the hillsides around Longyearbyen.

claims.quote: In nineteen oh one, an American businessman called John Munro Longyear came to Svalbard on a cruise with his family. He met people prospecting for coal, took samples home, and liked what he found.
claims.statement: American businessman John Munro Longyear visited Svalbard on a cruise with his family in 1901, met coal prospectors and took coal samples home with positive results.

claims.quote: In nineteen oh six his Arctic Coal Company started mining here. The town was called Longyear City until nineteen twenty-six.
claims.statement: Longyear's Arctic Coal Company began coal mining at Longyearbyen in 1906; the town was known as Longyear City until 1926.

claims.quote: The American company ran into money trouble, and in nineteen sixteen the Norwegian company Store Norske bought the mines. The Norwegian state became an owner in the nineteen thirties and now owns the company outright.
claims.statement: After financial difficulties, the Arctic Coal Company's mines were bought by Store Norske in 1916; the Norwegian state became an owner in the 1930s and now wholly owns Store Norske.

claims.quote: For more than a hundred years, coal was the reason this town had lights, heat and jobs.
claims.statement: For over a century, coal mining was the economic basis of Longyearbyen, supplying jobs and energy.

claims.quote: At the end of June twenty twenty-five, Mine Seven, the last Norwegian coal mine on Svalbard, closed.
claims.statement: Mine 7, the last Norwegian coal mine on Svalbard, closed at the end of June 2025.

claims.quote: In February nineteen twenty, a treaty signed in Paris recognised Norway's sovereignty over Svalbard, but with conditions. Norway has to treat citizens and companies from the countries that signed it equally. Today the treaty has forty-eight parties.
claims.statement: The Svalbard Treaty, signed in Paris on 9 February 1920, recognises Norwegian sovereignty but obliges Norway to ensure equal rights for citizens and companies of the parties; it now has 48 parties.

claims.quote: according to the Governor of Svalbard, you do not need a visa or a Norwegian residence permit to come here. The Norwegian Immigration Act does not apply.
claims.statement: According to the Governor of Svalbard, no visa or Norwegian work or residence permit is needed to travel to Svalbard, because the Immigration Act does not apply there.

claims.quote: You must be able to support yourself. Most housing is provided by employers, nearly all the land belongs to the state, and the Governor can turn away people who do not meet the requirements.
claims.statement: Residents of Svalbard must be able to support themselves; most housing is provided by employers, the state owns nearly all land, and the Governor may refuse entry or residence to those who do not meet the requirements.

claims.quote: According to the Governor of Svalbard, anyone travelling outside the settlements must carry suitable means of scaring off polar bears, and the Governor also recommends carrying a firearm.
claims.statement: According to the Governor of Svalbard, anyone travelling outside the settlements must carry suitable means of scaring off polar bears, and carrying firearms is recommended.

claims.quote: Seven miners who died in the Spanish flu pandemic of nineteen eighteen are buried there.
claims.statement: Longyearbyen's graveyard holds seven Norwegian miners who died in the 1918 Spanish flu pandemic.

claims.quote: Because of the permafrost, bodies in this ground do not decompose the way they would elsewhere, and the frozen soil slowly pushes coffins upward. Since around nineteen fifty, the cemetery has not taken new burials, and people who die here are taken to the mainland to be buried.
claims.statement: Because permafrost preserves bodies and heaving brings coffins toward the surface, Longyearbyen's cemetery stopped accepting new burials around 1950, and those who die there are buried on the Norwegian mainland.

claims.quote: You may have heard that dying is illegal in Longyearbyen. It is not.
claims.statement: There is no law making it illegal to die in Longyearbyen; the restriction concerns burials in its cemetery.

claims.quote: In the late nineteen nineties, researchers even studied the remains of those miners, hoping to learn about the flu virus.
claims.statement: In the late 1990s, researchers examined the remains of the 1918 flu victims buried in Longyearbyen, hoping to find samples of the influenza virus.

claims.quote: On the eighth of September, nineteen forty-three, the German navy almost completely destroyed it. It was rebuilt after the war.
claims.statement: The German navy almost completely destroyed Longyearbyen on 8 September 1943; the town was rebuilt after the Second World War.

claims.quote: This is where the Svalbard Global Seed Vault has kept backup copies of the world's crop seeds since it opened in twenty oh eight. It now holds more than a million seed samples, according to the vault's own figures quoted by travel guides.
claims.statement: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault near Longyearbyen opened in 2008 to store backup copies of crop seeds and now holds more than one million seed samples.

claims.quote: The University Centre in Svalbard brings students to study the Arctic. Tourism brings visitors for the midnight sun, the northern lights and the glaciers.
claims.statement: Research and education, including the University Centre in Svalbard, and tourism have become important parts of Longyearbyen's economy.

claims.quote: People often take their shoes off at the door, even in shops and hotels
claims.statement: In Longyearbyen it is common to leave shoes by the door, and slippers are often provided indoors.

claims.quote: There is a hospital, a school and a sports centre, all of which can claim to be the northernmost of their kind. There are no roads connecting Svalbard's settlements
claims.statement: Longyearbyen has a hospital, school and recreation centre that are the northernmost of their kind, and there are no roads between Svalbard's settlements.

claims.quote: In Longyearbyen the polar night lasts from about the twenty-sixth of October until about the fifteenth of February.
claims.statement: In Longyearbyen, the polar night lasts from about 26 October to 15 February.

claims.quote: The midnight sun lasts from about the twentieth of April until about the twenty-third of August.
claims.statement: In Longyearbyen, the midnight sun lasts from about 20 April to 23 August.
